Define the attribution gap: The paper formalizes the "attribution gap" as the logical space between output manifestation and structural instantiation, highlighting the inferential risks of conflating performance with ontology. Introduce a binary admissibility framework: The paper proposes a binary classification function to determine whether structural attribution is admissible for a system, based on necessary conditions and asymmetrical falsification. Operationalize the invariance principle: The paper defines the reset operator as an identity-preserving transformation to test whether a property is stable across a system's internal state-space, which is a necessary condition for structural attribution. Prevent category errors in AI evaluation: The framework aims to prevent the common error of treating behavioral success as evidence of system-level properties, such as understanding or epistemic subjecthood, without meeting the necessary logical conditions. Reframe AI evaluation: The paper proposes shifting the focus of AI evaluation from task performance to testing stability and invariance under identity-preserving transformations, ensuring that structural attribution is disciplined and logically warranted. sources.title: 'Could kill us all': Another AI employee quits, sounds alarm over safety
passages: Another AI employee has quit over safety concerns, adding to a growing list of researchers and employees who have publicly warned that the race to develop increasingly powerful AI systems is moving too fast.Jacob Coxon, a 27-year-old researcher who spent the past three years conducting pretraining research at OpenAI and Anthropic, announced his resignation from Anthropic in a post on X.

“Accepting this race and entering the ‘endgame’ is a hubristic gamble that should not be launched from a private company’s Slack,” he said.He called for greater coordination between AI companies and governments and said a temporary ban on improving model capabilities could be among the measures needed to prevent a global race.His comments were backed by Anthropic researcher Evan Hubinger, who wrote: “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” Hubinger later said he personally puts the chance of this happening over the next decade at under 10%.Anthropic said it has “always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks” and that it continues to build models with strong safeguards.The latest resignation comes as AI leaders themselves acknowledge growing safety concerns.

Several employees at major AI companies have quit or spoken out over fears that advances in AI could outpace efforts to keep the systems under human control.In July, nearly 1,400 AI company employees signed an open letter calling for stronger regulation and a slower pace of development to improve AI safety, according to a CNN report.Coxon said that while the risks are understood at Anthropic, the company remains caught in a race with other AI developers.

story.title: An OpenAI safety employee has quit and is sounding the alarm

facts.text: David Robinson used to write the safety reports that accompanied every major model release at OpenAI.
A flurry of A.I. researchers have been sounding the alarm as they walk out of major companies.
A slew of high-profile employees have quit Open-AI, anthropic and X-A.I. in the past few days.

Shilpa Ranipeta has the details. #AI #ArtificialIntelligence #AIResearch #TechNews #OpenAI #Anthropic #xAI #AIEthics #AISafety #TechIndustry #MachineLearning #FutureOfAI #BigTech #Innovation #EmergingTech #CNBCTV18Digital

One of the most persistent problems in today’s AI debate is what I call the attribution gap: the mismatch between what we observe in a system’s outputs and what actually constitutes the system itself.
Impressive performance makes this easy to miss.
A model produces fluent language, and we quickly start talking as if it understands, thinks, or means something.
In practice, high performance becomes a shortcut to ontology. - But how do we know a system possesses a property, rather than merely producing behavior consistent with it?
Why this matters: This is not an attack on AI’s usefulness.
It is a call for stricter conceptual hygiene.

If we attribute properties to systems, we should be explicit about the logical conditions that make such attribution admissible. → For the ontological consequences of this framework, see: Artificial Intelligence as Instrumental Extension - an Ontological Clarification (Hansen, 2026).
Discussion: Are we too quick to attribute human-like properties to AI based on output alone?

What conditions should be satisfied before we talk about systems as if they “understand”? #ArtificialIntelligence #Ontology #PhilosophyOfTech #MachineLearning #StructuralAttribution #AITheory #ConceptualHygiene #Epistemology

Washington (United States) (AFP) – President Donald Trump is expected to name Jay Clayton, the US director of national intelligence, as the White House's new AI czar, CNN and other US media reported Friday.
Trump tapped Clayton to lead federal prosecutors in Manhattan at the start of his second term, and the Senate confirmed him as intelligence chief in July.

Trump said last month he would create an "AI Force" modeled on the Space Force he established during his first term, and name a czar to coordinate federal AI efforts.
A longtime Wall Street lawyer, Clayton represented Goldman Sachs during the 2008 financial crisis and Barclays in its purchase of Lehman Brothers' assets.
Trump has resisted tighter AI regulation, arguing a slowdown could hand Chinese firms an advantage and that federal law enforcement can deal with bad actors misusing the technology.
Tech bosses at a White House meeting this week signed a commitment to self-police AI, an accord Trump described as "morally binding."
He chaired the Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump's first term, where he largely took a pro-business stance but brought enforcement cases against the nascent crypto industry.
Crypto entrepreneurs have since become major Trump backers.

passages: President Trump is expected to name Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as the White House’s artificial intelligence czar, according to a source familiar with the matter.
“Superintelligence is a national security issue,” Clayton said, using the term the Trump administration has formally adopted to refer to AI.

Trump’s selection of Clayton comes after a groundswell of concern about the consequences associated with AI development following warnings by employees at some of the top AI companies about the technology putting humanity at risk.
Trump has largely brushed off these threats, including after his meeting with AI giants, pushing back on calls to implement stronger safety regulations.

extraction.body: President Trump is expected to name Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as the White House’s artificial intelligence czar, according to a source familiar with the matter. The president teased the move this week and will most likely announce it on social media as early as Friday, the source said. It comes after a lengthy meeting with executives of leading technology companies at the White House on Tuesday, which Clayton attended. Clayton, who oversees the nation’s spy agencies as the director of national intelligence, would take on the AI responsibility alongside his current role. The president could announce his decision about Clayton, who is director of national intelligence, as early as Friday, one of the sources said. Trump announced last month that he was planning to create an “AI Force” and name an AI czar as the government faces growing calls to impose guardrails on the technology’s rapid development. Clayton succeeded Bill Pulte, a controversial housing executive with no national security experience whom Trump installed as acting director for a 40-day tenure. When asked about AI during his confirmation hearing, Clayton said the technology is a “game changer” and that it’s “not only an opportunity but a threat.” “When something’s both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it,” Clayton said. Venture capitalist David Sacks previously served as Trump’s AI and cryptocurrency czar until March 2026, when he stepped down after reaching his time limit as a special government employee. He now co-chairs the president’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology. Sacks has continued to have considerable influence on the president when it comes to AI issues. On Tuesday, Trump told reporters that he was “very close to making a decision,” regarding his pick for the role. “I’ll be naming one, I’d say, over the next three or four days.” Trump added that he first wanted to check with “the companies” as well as House GOP leadership in Congress before making his decision. The president has made clear that he considers outpacing China and preserving AI-driven economic gains a higher priority than addressing growing public concerns, and previously referred to fears over AI as being a “hoax.”

Russia Strikes Another Major Bridge in Ukraine Capital A Russian strike targeted a major bridge in Kyiv, its mayor said Saturday, in another attack on Ukrainian infrastructure that has brought traffic chaos to the capital. The attack on the Northern Bridge, which followed a drone alert, came a day after the Southern Bridge was hit in a wave of strikes that city officials say is "tearing Kyiv apart". The grinding conflict, which began with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, has largely focused on ground fighting in the east, with Kyiv mostly spared from the devastation wrought near the frontline, AFP said. "Jamshidi was sentenced to death on charges of moharebeh through brandishing and firing a firearm, as well as conspiracy and collusion against national security," Iran's judiciary said, using the legal term moharebeh to mean "waging war against God". The judiciary's Mizan Online website said he was also found guilty of offences not related to the protests, including "fraud, making threats, theft, possession and carrying of an illegal military-grade weapon". Other charges included "complicity in kidnapping, brandishing a weapon to intimidate, and intentional infliction of bodily harm". Mizan said Jamshidi was "active" during the demonstrations, which were sparked in December last year by grievances over living costs in Iran, but peaked on January 8 and 9 with huge rallies. Iranian authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths in the unrest, attributing the violence to "terrorist acts" orchestrated by the United States and Israel. Foreign-based NGOs however maintain that Iranian security forces fired on protesters. US President Donald Trump threatened at the time to intervene militarily in Iran. The president could announce his decision about Clayton, who is director of national intelligence, as early as Friday, one of the sources said. Trump announced last month that he was planning to create an “AI Force” and name an AI czar as the government faces growing calls to impose guardrails on the technology’s rapid development. Trump gathered several AI and technology CEOs at the White House on Tuesday for a meeting that culminated in the signing of a new commitment aimed at better “self-policing” their companies’ AI models. Trump previously told Axios that Clayton would be a good AI czar. CBS News first reported that Clayton was the frontrunner for the position. A White House official told CNN, “Any personnel announcement will be announced directly by the President. Any reporting until then is baseless speculation.” Clayton, who previously served as the top federal prosecutor in Manhattan and led the Securities and Exchange Commission during the majority of Trump’s first term, is expected to remain in his role as director of national intelligence, the sources said. He was confirmed by the Senate in July to lead the US intelligence community. Clayton succeeded Bill Pulte, a controversial housing executive with no national security experience whom Trump installed as acting director for a 40-day tenure. When asked about AI during his confirmation hearing, Clayton said the technology is a “game changer” and that it’s “not only an opportunity but a threat.” “When something’s both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it,” Clayton said. Venture capitalist David Sacks previously served as Trump’s AI and cryptocurrency czar until March 2026, when he stepped down after reaching his time limit as a special government employee. He now co-chairs the president’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology. Sacks has continued to have considerable influence on the president when it comes to AI issues. On Tuesday, Trump told reporters that he was “very close to making a decision,” regarding his pick for the role. “I’ll be naming one, I’d say, over the next three or four days.” Trump added that he first wanted to check with “the companies” as well as House GOP leadership in Congress before making his decision. The president has made clear that he considers outpacing China and preserving AI-driven economic gains a higher priority than addressing growing public concerns, and previously referred to fears over AI as being a “hoax.”

facts.text: CBS News reported a day earlier that Clayton was the likely pick and that the administration had discussed keeping him in his intelligence post, with Trump expected to make a final decision shortly.

Washington (United States) (AFP) – President Donald Trump is expected to name Jay Clayton, the US director of national intelligence, as the White House's new AI czar, CNN and other US media reported Friday.
Trump tapped Clayton to lead federal prosecutors in Manhattan at the start of his second term, and the Senate confirmed him as intelligence chief in July.

Trump said last month he would create an "AI Force" modeled on the Space Force he established during his first term, and name a czar to coordinate federal AI efforts.
A longtime Wall Street lawyer, Clayton represented Goldman Sachs during the 2008 financial crisis and Barclays in its purchase of Lehman Brothers' assets.
Trump has resisted tighter AI regulation, arguing a slowdown could hand Chinese firms an advantage and that federal law enforcement can deal with bad actors misusing the technology.
Tech bosses at a White House meeting this week signed a commitment to self-police AI, an accord Trump described as "morally binding."
He chaired the Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump's first term, where he largely took a pro-business stance but brought enforcement cases against the nascent crypto industry.
Crypto entrepreneurs have since become major Trump backers.
President Trump is expected to name Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as the White House’s artificial intelligence czar, according to a source familiar with the matter.
“Superintelligence is a national security issue,” Clayton said, using the term the Trump administration has formally adopted to refer to AI.

Trump’s selection of Clayton comes after a groundswell of concern about the consequences associated with AI development following warnings by employees at some of the top AI companies about the technology putting humanity at risk.
Trump has largely brushed off these threats, including after his meeting with AI giants, pushing back on calls to implement stronger safety regulations.
President Donald Trump is expected to pick Jay Clayton to be the White House’s new czar of artificial intelligence, two sources familiar with the discussion told CNN.
Trump announced last month that he was planning to create an “AI Force” and name an AI czar as the government faces growing calls to impose guardrails on the technology’s rapid development.
Trump previously told Axios that Clayton would be a good AI czar.
Clayton succeeded Bill Pulte, a controversial housing executive with no national security experience whom Trump installed as acting director for a 40-day tenure.
Venture capitalist David Sacks previously served as Trump’s AI and cryptocurrency czar until March 2026, when he stepped down after reaching his time limit as a special government employee.
“I’ll be naming one, I’d say, over the next three or four days.” Trump added that he first wanted to check with “the companies” as well as House GOP leadership in Congress before making his decision.

passages: Nat Friedman, who leads product at Meta Superintelligence Labs, has announced Muse Gadgets, an open source ESP32 firmware and Linux SDK that lets anyone build hardware devices that work with the company’s personal AI agent .
Meta has manufactured a batch of 5,000 Home Links, which Friedman says should be ready to ship in a few weeks.
They are free for Muse subscribers while supplies last.
According to the Gadgets site, the offer is limited to subscribers in the United States, with one per subscriber, and claiming a unit only holds a place in line rather than placing an order.
All of the code for Home Link is open source too.
Developers can grab an API token from the Muse Gadgets site and point their coding agent of choice at the GitHub repository to start building peripherals.
Muse launched on September 8 as Meta’s first consumer-facing agentic app, and has since added commerce tie-ups with Shopify, PayPal, Instacart and Expedia.
Friedman has also acknowledged that Muse was heavily inspired by OpenClaw, the open source agent created by Peter Steinberger, who later joined OpenAI .
Meta is taking some big bets with its AI agent, Muse.
Meta says community-built skills could let Muse turn on a light, control a TV or send a document to a printer, depending on a user’s setup.
Opening up the hardware side follows a similar playbook to OpenClaw’s: put the code in the hands of tinkerers and see what they come up with.
Muse Gadgets is available at gadgets.muse.ai, and the SDK is on GitHub at facebookincubator/muse-gadget-sdk.

extraction.body: Meta is taking some big bets with its AI agent, Muse. Meta now wants Muse to leave the screen. Nat Friedman, who leads product at Meta Superintelligence Labs, has announced Muse Gadgets, an open source ESP32 firmware and Linux SDK that lets anyone build hardware devices that work with the company’s personal AI agent . Developers can grab an API token from the Muse Gadgets site and point their coding agent of choice at the GitHub repository to start building peripherals. The code is released under the Apache 2.0 license. The ESP32 SDK is aimed at off-the-shelf microcontroller boards. Builders can add a screen to show images, audio in and out, or other sensors. The Linux SDK, meanwhile, turns a spare Raspberry Pi or other Linux machine into a Muse gadget, with custom commands that can let Muse handle sysadmin chores or work with a Home Assistant setup. Meta has listed a number of project ideas to get people started. One is a round AMOLED touchscreen from Waveshare, which comes with push-to-talk, a speaker, a microphone and a battery. Another is Seeed’s reTerminal E1002, a colour e-ink display that could show a morning briefing, reminders or a shopping list. M5Stack’s pocket-sized StickS3 shows Muse’s status on a colour screen, while the AiPi Lite is a small desk companion that answers out loud and shows pictures. Home Assistant’s Voice Preview Edition, meanwhile, pairs push-to-talk with an LED ring that shows Muse’s status. An HDMI stick that would let Muse put content on a TV screen is listed as coming soon. Meta also runs a community Discord where builders can share projects, and says it may feature the best ones on the Gadgets site. Meta has also built a gadget of its own. Muse Home Link is a small USB-C powered device that connects Muse to a user’s home network, so the agent can talk to smart home devices such as TVs and speakers, and to anything else that exposes an HTTP interface. Meta says community-built skills could let Muse turn on a light, control a TV or send a document to a printer, depending on a user’s setup. Meta has manufactured a batch of 5,000 Home Links, which Friedman says should be ready to ship in a few weeks. They are free for Muse subscribers while supplies last. According to the Gadgets site, the offer is limited to subscribers in the United States, with one per subscriber, and claiming a unit only holds a place in line rather than placing an order. All of the code for Home Link is open source too. The move extends a product that has had a busy few weeks. Muse launched on September 8 as Meta’s first consumer-facing agentic app, and has since added commerce tie-ups with Shopify, PayPal, Instacart and Expedia. It has also drawn comparisons with OpenAI’s rival agents, to the point that OpenAI’s CFO mistakenly called her company’s new Dots agents “Muse” in a TV interview. Friedman has also acknowledged that Muse was heavily inspired by OpenClaw, the open source agent created by Peter Steinberger, who later joined OpenAI . Opening up the hardware side follows a similar playbook to OpenClaw’s: put the code in the hands of tinkerers and see what they come up with. The Gadgets site is upfront that this is a hacker project, warning that side effects of tinkering may include bricked boards and voided warranties. Muse Gadgets is available at gadgets.muse.ai, and the SDK is on GitHub at facebookincubator/muse-gadget-sdk.

extraction.body: Meta's Muse is still gaining continuous momentum. This newly launched personal AI Agent has already become a key product in Meta's AI strategy this year. Different from traditional chatbots, Muse is designed as an intelligent assistant that can perform tasks on behalf of users: processing emails, shopping, planning itineraries, and even completing a number of complex operations continuously in the background. And just now, Meta has announced a new move: officially launching the Muse Gadgets open source project to fully delegate hardware capabilities, enabling global makers and developers to build exclusive peripheral hardware devices for Muse. According to the information released by Meta, developers can use the ESP32 development board to run the Muse firmware, or use the Linux SDK to connect more complex devices, which means that developers can not only deploy the Muse interaction logic on low-cost microcontrollers, but also directly run the Muse client on more powerful edge computing devices such as Raspberry Pi 5. The official side has also listed a variety of highly practical DIY form references: HDMI Display Stick / Large Screen Expansion: Project the interface or interaction of the Muse Agent directly to a TV or external monitor. Touch-controlled Handheld Pendant: Make a portable interactive terminal similar to Muse Charm, so that you can talk to the Agent at any time without wearing smart glasses. For developers who want to get started and try it out, you can follow the steps below to start building your own exclusive Muse peripheral right now: At the same time, Meta has also launched an official device: Muse Home Link, a small USB-C powered device, which allows Muse to connect to your home network to communicate with smart home devices, such as TVs, speakers, and any devices that support HTTPS interfaces, further bringing the AI Agent into real life scenarios. The official stated that 5000 units of Muse Home Link have been produced in the first trial production run, and shipments are expected to start in a few weeks. While stocks are sufficient, the devices will be distributed directly for free to eligible Muse subscription users for experience. In response to everyone's curiosity about why Meta took the open source move, Alexandr Wang said, "First of all, building all kinds of small gadgets is fun in itself. Secondly, we hope to unlock the creativity of developers and let everyone explore all kinds of brand new, even crazy ideas. We believe that Muse is at a special moment, it provides unlimited possibilities for people to create new types of hardware devices, and we are very much looking forward to seeing what kind of works everyone will end up building!" From this perspective, Meta seems to hope that Muse is not just an official product, but an extensible platform. As soon as the project was released, it immediately attracted the attention of netizens, and even some netizens got started and DIYed their own Muse devices. There are many more user cases like this. Through this attempt of Muse, we can also see a change in the Agent era: In the past, the development path of smart hardware was usually: Company designs hardware — Users purchase devices — Develop applications. But AI Agent may move towards another model: The company provides models and Agent capabilities — Developers create devices of various forms. In fact, starting from AI Pin, the industry has made a lot of explorations in AI hardware, and has tried to replace the mobile phone entry through independent devices, but many products are affected by problems such as functional restrictions and poor interactive experience. Now, manufacturers seem to be changing their minds: directly build a powerful AI Agent first, and then let it enter different hardware. Meta's route may be exactly this: Muse is responsible for the intelligent capabilities, and developers are responsible for creating various carriers. In the future, Muse may exist in smartphones, smart glasses, various home devices, and even new hardware created by developers... So what about you, what do you think of Meta's this attempt? coreStoryFacts.text: Meta now lets you make your own Muse gadgets that feature the company’s new AI agent with code that the company open sourced.
“Muse gadgets are open source devices you build yourself,” Meta says.
With the Muse Home Link, you use community-built skills to have the AI agent “turn on a light, control your TV, send a document to a printer, and more, depending on your setup,” Meta says.

Nat Friedman, who leads product at Meta Superintelligence Labs, has announced Muse Gadgets, an open source ESP32 firmware and Linux SDK that lets anyone build hardware devices that work with the company’s personal AI agent .
Meta has manufactured a batch of 5,000 Home Links, which Friedman says should be ready to ship in a few weeks.
They are free for Muse subscribers while supplies last.
According to the Gadgets site, the offer is limited to subscribers in the United States, with one per subscriber, and claiming a unit only holds a place in line rather than placing an order.
All of the code for Home Link is open source too.
Developers can grab an API token from the Muse Gadgets site and point their coding agent of choice at the GitHub repository to start building peripherals.
Muse launched on September 8 as Meta’s first consumer-facing agentic app, and has since added commerce tie-ups with Shopify, PayPal, Instacart and Expedia.
Friedman has also acknowledged that Muse was heavily inspired by OpenClaw, the open source agent created by Peter Steinberger, who later joined OpenAI .
Meta is taking some big bets with its AI agent, Muse.
Meta says community-built skills could let Muse turn on a light, control a TV or send a document to a printer, depending on a user’s setup.
Opening up the hardware side follows a similar playbook to OpenClaw’s: put the code in the hands of tinkerers and see what they come up with.
Muse Gadgets is available at gadgets.muse.ai, and the SDK is on GitHub at facebookincubator/muse-gadget-sdk.

And just now, Meta has announced a new move: officially launching the Muse Gadgets open source project to fully delegate hardware capabilities, enabling global makers and developers to build exclusive peripheral hardware devices for Muse.
In response to everyone's curiosity about why Meta took the open source move, Alexandr Wang said, "First of all, building all kinds of small gadgets is fun in itself.

According to the information released by Meta, developers can use the ESP32 development board to run the Muse firmware, or use the Linux SDK to connect more complex devices, which means that developers can not only deploy the Muse interaction logic on low-cost microcontrollers, but also directly run the Muse client on more powerful edge computing devices such as Raspberry Pi 5.
For developers who want to get started and try it out, you can follow the steps below to start building your own exclusive Muse peripheral right now:

We believe that Muse is at a special moment, it provides unlimited possibilities for people to create new types of hardware devices, and we are very much looking forward to seeing what kind of works everyone will end up building!"
Meta's route may be exactly this: Muse is responsible for the intelligent capabilities, and developers are responsible for creating various carriers.
In the future, Muse may exist in smartphones, smart glasses, various home devices, and even new hardware created by developers...

At the same time, Meta has also launched an official device: Muse Home Link, a small USB-C powered device, which allows Muse to connect to your home network to communicate with smart home devices, such as TVs, speakers, and any devices that support HTTPS interfaces, further bringing the AI Agent into real life scenarios.
Meta has open-sourced the code for its Muse Gadgets, allowing developers and enthusiasts to build their own hardware devices featuring the company’s Muse AI agent.

extraction.body: Meta is taking some big bets with its AI agent, Muse. Meta now wants Muse to leave the screen. Nat Friedman, who leads product at Meta Superintelligence Labs, has announced Muse Gadgets, an open source ESP32 firmware and Linux SDK that lets anyone build hardware devices that work with the company’s personal AI agent . Developers can grab an API token from the Muse Gadgets site and point their coding agent of choice at the GitHub repository to start building peripherals. The code is released under the Apache 2.0 license. The ESP32 SDK is aimed at off-the-shelf microcontroller boards. Builders can add a screen to show images, audio in and out, or other sensors. The Linux SDK, meanwhile, turns a spare Raspberry Pi or other Linux machine into a Muse gadget, with custom commands that can let Muse handle sysadmin chores or work with a Home Assistant setup. Meta has listed a number of project ideas to get people started. One is a round AMOLED touchscreen from Waveshare, which comes with push-to-talk, a speaker, a microphone and a battery. Another is Seeed’s reTerminal E1002, a colour e-ink display that could show a morning briefing, reminders or a shopping list. M5Stack’s pocket-sized StickS3 shows Muse’s status on a colour screen, while the AiPi Lite is a small desk companion that answers out loud and shows pictures. Home Assistant’s Voice Preview Edition, meanwhile, pairs push-to-talk with an LED ring that shows Muse’s status. An HDMI stick that would let Muse put content on a TV screen is listed as coming soon. Meta also runs a community Discord where builders can share projects, and says it may feature the best ones on the Gadgets site. Meta has also built a gadget of its own. Muse Home Link is a small USB-C powered device that connects Muse to a user’s home network, so the agent can talk to smart home devices such as TVs and speakers, and to anything else that exposes an HTTP interface. Meta says community-built skills could let Muse turn on a light, control a TV or send a document to a printer, depending on a user’s setup. Meta has manufactured a batch of 5,000 Home Links, which Friedman says should be ready to ship in a few weeks. They are free for Muse subscribers while supplies last. According to the Gadgets site, the offer is limited to subscribers in the United States, with one per subscriber, and claiming a unit only holds a place in line rather than placing an order. All of the code for Home Link is open source too. The move extends a product that has had a busy few weeks. Muse launched on September 8 as Meta’s first consumer-facing agentic app, and has since added commerce tie-ups with Shopify, PayPal, Instacart and Expedia. It has also drawn comparisons with OpenAI’s rival agents, to the point that OpenAI’s CFO mistakenly called her company’s new Dots agents “Muse” in a TV interview. Friedman has also acknowledged that Muse was heavily inspired by OpenClaw, the open source agent created by Peter Steinberger, who later joined OpenAI . Opening up the hardware side follows a similar playbook to OpenClaw’s: put the code in the hands of tinkerers and see what they come up with. The Gadgets site is upfront that this is a hacker project, warning that side effects of tinkering may include bricked boards and voided warranties. Muse Gadgets is available at gadgets.muse.ai, and the SDK is on GitHub at facebookincubator/muse-gadget-sdk.

extraction.body: Meta's Muse is still gaining continuous momentum. This newly launched personal AI Agent has already become a key product in Meta's AI strategy this year. Different from traditional chatbots, Muse is designed as an intelligent assistant that can perform tasks on behalf of users: processing emails, shopping, planning itineraries, and even completing a number of complex operations continuously in the background. And just now, Meta has announced a new move: officially launching the Muse Gadgets open source project to fully delegate hardware capabilities, enabling global makers and developers to build exclusive peripheral hardware devices for Muse. According to the information released by Meta, developers can use the ESP32 development board to run the Muse firmware, or use the Linux SDK to connect more complex devices, which means that developers can not only deploy the Muse interaction logic on low-cost microcontrollers, but also directly run the Muse client on more powerful edge computing devices such as Raspberry Pi 5. The official side has also listed a variety of highly practical DIY form references: HDMI Display Stick / Large Screen Expansion: Project the interface or interaction of the Muse Agent directly to a TV or external monitor. Touch-controlled Handheld Pendant: Make a portable interactive terminal similar to Muse Charm, so that you can talk to the Agent at any time without wearing smart glasses. For developers who want to get started and try it out, you can follow the steps below to start building your own exclusive Muse peripheral right now: At the same time, Meta has also launched an official device: Muse Home Link, a small USB-C powered device, which allows Muse to connect to your home network to communicate with smart home devices, such as TVs, speakers, and any devices that support HTTPS interfaces, further bringing the AI Agent into real life scenarios. The official stated that 5000 units of Muse Home Link have been produced in the first trial production run, and shipments are expected to start in a few weeks. While stocks are sufficient, the devices will be distributed directly for free to eligible Muse subscription users for experience. In response to everyone's curiosity about why Meta took the open source move, Alexandr Wang said, "First of all, building all kinds of small gadgets is fun in itself. Secondly, we hope to unlock the creativity of developers and let everyone explore all kinds of brand new, even crazy ideas. We believe that Muse is at a special moment, it provides unlimited possibilities for people to create new types of hardware devices, and we are very much looking forward to seeing what kind of works everyone will end up building!" From this perspective, Meta seems to hope that Muse is not just an official product, but an extensible platform. As soon as the project was released, it immediately attracted the attention of netizens, and even some netizens got started and DIYed their own Muse devices. There are many more user cases like this. Through this attempt of Muse, we can also see a change in the Agent era: In the past, the development path of smart hardware was usually: Company designs hardware — Users purchase devices — Develop applications. But AI Agent may move towards another model: The company provides models and Agent capabilities — Developers create devices of various forms. In fact, starting from AI Pin, the industry has made a lot of explorations in AI hardware, and has tried to replace the mobile phone entry through independent devices, but many products are affected by problems such as functional restrictions and poor interactive experience. Now, manufacturers seem to be changing their minds: directly build a powerful AI Agent first, and then let it enter different hardware. Meta's route may be exactly this: Muse is responsible for the intelligent capabilities, and developers are responsible for creating various carriers. In the future, Muse may exist in smartphones, smart glasses, various home devices, and even new hardware created by developers... So what about you, what do you think of Meta's this attempt? story.title: Meta open sources code to let you make Muse AI gadgets

facts.text: Meta now lets you make your own Muse gadgets that feature the company’s new AI agent with code that the company open sourced.
“Muse gadgets are open source devices you build yourself,” Meta says.
With the Muse Home Link, you use community-built skills to have the AI agent “turn on a light, control your TV, send a document to a printer, and more, depending on your setup,” Meta says.

Nat Friedman, who leads product at Meta Superintelligence Labs, has announced Muse Gadgets, an open source ESP32 firmware and Linux SDK that lets anyone build hardware devices that work with the company’s personal AI agent .
Meta has manufactured a batch of 5,000 Home Links, which Friedman says should be ready to ship in a few weeks.
They are free for Muse subscribers while supplies last.
According to the Gadgets site, the offer is limited to subscribers in the United States, with one per subscriber, and claiming a unit only holds a place in line rather than placing an order.
All of the code for Home Link is open source too.
Developers can grab an API token from the Muse Gadgets site and point their coding agent of choice at the GitHub repository to start building peripherals.
Muse launched on September 8 as Meta’s first consumer-facing agentic app, and has since added commerce tie-ups with Shopify, PayPal, Instacart and Expedia.
Friedman has also acknowledged that Muse was heavily inspired by OpenClaw, the open source agent created by Peter Steinberger, who later joined OpenAI .
Meta is taking some big bets with its AI agent, Muse.
Meta says community-built skills could let Muse turn on a light, control a TV or send a document to a printer, depending on a user’s setup.
Opening up the hardware side follows a similar playbook to OpenClaw’s: put the code in the hands of tinkerers and see what they come up with.
Muse Gadgets is available at gadgets.muse.ai, and the SDK is on GitHub at facebookincubator/muse-gadget-sdk.

Broadcom (NASDAQ: AVGO) is providing hardware that could rival Nvidia 's graphics processing units ( GPUs) , while Applied Digital (NASDAQ: APLD) is building the physical infrastructure that hyperscalers need to run it all. So for investors who are looking for promising AI bets other than Palantir, these two stocks deserve a closer look. Missed AI’s "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we’re only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Nvidia might dominate the conversation when it comes to GPUs, but Broadcom is becoming an increasingly important player in AI infrastructure . But chips are only part of the equation. As AI computing requirements continue to grow, the industry also needs to keep adding physical infrastructure. That's where Applied Digital comes into the picture. Applied Digital offers a different way to participate in the AI boom. Instead of designing chips or developing AI models, the company builds and runs the data centers that power AI workloads. It has been expanding its portfolio of AI campuses, attracting major customers through long-term lease agreements that provide it with strong visibility into its future revenues. It has secured three deals with an investment-grade hyperscaler across different campuses, bringing its total contracted capacity to $36 billion. Moreover, Applied Digital continues to make progress on its existing projects. Its Polaris Forge 1 campus in North Dakota has already kicked off operations, and additional capacity will keep coming online as construction continues. The company also secured further financing to expand its data center portfolio, helping turn its pipeline into operational facilities. Another important development was its move to hive off its cloud services business into a new public company, ChronoScale (NASDAQ: CHRN) . This will allow Applied Digital to focus more on developing and running large-scale AI campuses. That should help strengthen its business, especially as hyperscalers race to secure more computing capacity to train and run advanced AI models. Although Broadcom and Applied Digital are in different parts of the AI supply chain, both stand to benefit from the huge investments being made in the technology. For investors who want a steadier way to play the AI theme than Palantir offers, Broadcom's diversified chip and software business, along with its exposure to surging demand for custom AI chips and networking technology, makes it the safer of these two picks. Applied Digital, on the other hand, is the higher-risk, higher-reward option, as it's betting big on building the data centers needed to power the next generation of AI. passages: WASHINGTON, Oct 2 (Reuters) – The Federal Aviation Administration said on Friday that a panel of experts had determined a software glitch in some Boeing 737 MAX flight computers poses no safety concern, clearing the way ​for approval of a larger version of the best-selling narrow-body jet.
It should also ease concerns at airlines that fly the MAX 7, which uses the same software and was certified by the FAA in August.
Jefferies said in a research note the decision allows the MAX 10 to be certified before the end of the year and estimated Boeing has nearly 1,500 MAX 10s ⁠on order from airlines.

Boeing said it “will continue to follow the lead of the FAA as our ⁠engineers work on the next software update.” Boeing ⁠added it is working directly with airlines to formalize a procedure ​that will allow pilots “to re-enable automated vertical navigation should this situation occur.”

An FAA official said Boeing will issue ​a bulletin to ⁠airlines on how to recognize and respond to the situation should it occur, and the FAA will issue a Special Airworthiness Information Bulletin to US airlines and foreign regulators to ensure they’re aware of Boeing’s bulletin.

passages: Boeing’s 737 Max 10 certification gets a boost after a Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) panel determined that a software glitch affecting certain 737 Max flight computers does not pose a safety risk.The FAA’s Corrective Action Review Board made the determination on Friday after examining the issue, which could occur when pilots abort a landing attempt.Following the report, Boeing shares rose 1.6% to $195.40 as of 2:47 p.m.
The smaller 737 Max 7 was certified in August with the affected software.
“The agency will also issue a special airworthiness information bulletin to US carriers and foreign regulators to ensure they’re aware of Boeing’s bulletin," the official said.
United has also said it is not accepting deliveries of new aircraft equipped with the glitch, while Southwest said recent and upcoming Max 8 deliveries would not have the malfunctioning software.

Boeing will issue a bulletin to airlines explaining how crews should respond if the malfunction occurs. “The agency will also issue a special airworthiness information bulletin to US carriers and foreign regulators to ensure they’re aware of Boeing’s bulletin," the official said. “We will continue to follow the lead of the FAA as our engineers work on the next software update,” Boeing said in a statement following the FAA’s determination. GE Aerospace, which supplies the software, said it supports the FAA’s decision and will continue working with Boeing on the update. The FAA’s decision removes a potential regulatory hurdle for Boeing’s 737 Max 10, the largest version of the Max family. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford had said earlier this week that certification of the aircraft would be delayed until the agency determined whether the software problem posed a safety risk. The smaller 737 Max 7 was certified in August with the affected software. The Max 10 is already years behind schedule and is important to Boeing’s efforts to generate cash and strengthen its balance sheet. Are airlines flying aircraft with the glitch? Boeing customers Southwest Airlines, United Airlines, American Airlines and Alaska Air have separately said they do not operate aircraft with the affected software version. United has also said it is not accepting deliveries of new aircraft equipped with the glitch, while Southwest said recent and upcoming Max 8 deliveries would not have the malfunctioning software.

extraction.body: Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person. You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later. While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space. Below are some of the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work. Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check. For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you. Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026. Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan. The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar. Fambot currently connects to Gmail and Google Calendar, with support for Outlook and Apple Calendar planned for the future. The company launched in beta in early September 2026 and has raised $3.5 million in pre-seed funding. The service is currently free during the beta period, but Fambot expects to eventually charge roughly the equivalent of a Netflix subscription. Folk is designed to be an AI assistant you can reach through iMessage, WhatsApp, and Telegram. It can remember personal context, manage reminders, research topics, track flights, handle email, and perform real-world tasks such as restaurant reservations. Instinct first made headlines after raising $350 million at a $2.5 billion valuation. In September 2026, it raised $1 billion , valuing it at $10 billion. The always-available agent can take actions on your behalf, rather than simply answer questions. Users can communicate with Instinct by text or voice and connect it to the apps and services they already use, such as email, calendar, Google Workspace, and more. The company says early users have used Instinct for tasks ranging from planning trips and buying groceries to booking tickets and cancelling subscriptions. In September, Instinct began giving users dedicated email addresses for their assistants. The idea is to let Instinct create and manage accounts on a user’s behalf without filling the user’s personal inbox. The agent can use its address to sign up for services, contact businesses, follow up on requests, and handle tasks that require an email account. (However, this level of autonomy has also raised concerns about privacy and security .) It’s also begun rolling out support for placing calls . Martin is a general-purpose personal assistant reachable through SMS as well as phone, WhatsApp, email, Slack, and its own iOS app. It can help manage calendars, email, reminders, tasks, notes, and communications. It can also act on behalf of users by sending messages or making phone calls, while providing daily summaries of what needs attention. It’s a bit on the pricier side, with subscriptions starting at $21 per month. Ohai is another family assistant focused on helping households manage the constant stream of information and tasks involved in everyday family life. Users can send messages, forward emails, or make voice requests, and the assistant can transform them into schedules, reminders, and plans. It can also coordinate calendars, household chores, and meals across multiple members of a family. It includes a free basic option, but also offers different subscriptions based on family size, starting at $9.99 per month. Similar to the other family-focused agents, the idea behind Ollie is that families already have the information they need, but it lives across school messages, calendars, task lists, and group chats. Ollie aims to bring those pieces together and keep them in sync. It can keep track of calendars, emails, reminders, tasks, and other household details, then deliver relevant information to users through text. Its biggest differentiator from other agents is that Ollie is one of the first mainstream, family-focused AI assistants to achieve SOC 2 compliance, a widely used security standard. Launched in June 2026, Ollie offers a free tier, as well as paid plans starting at $25 per month for 150 messages. A $100-per-month plan includes up to 1,000 messages. Orbits also has an AI assistant that is focused on the household. It works through both the Orbits app and text messaging, and can bring together calendars, lists, and conversations while also carrying out tasks for you. That can include searching the web, making purchases, booking restaurants, changing appointments, and requesting quotes for household services. Additionally, Orbits can remind family members about chores, communicate with service providers, and help coordinate responsibilities beyond the immediate household. There’s a free plan available, which offers features like 15 minutes of calls per month, or there are paid plans, including $25 per month for 30 minutes of calls and $100 per month for 60 minutes. Poke launched in March 2026 as a general-purpose assistant that you can reach through text messaging. It can handle tasks involving calendars, planning, health and fitness, smart-home controls, photos, and other everyday activities. Poke became particularly notable in June 2026 when Apple approved Poke as the first AI agent on the Apple Messages for Business platform. A month later, parent company The Interaction Company of California was acquired by AI coding startup Cognition in a deal valued in the low nine figures. Rene is an AI personal assistant designed to be a user’s “best contact” rather than another productivity agent. It’s text-based and can turn natural-language conversations into tasks, reminders, summaries, and other follow-up actions. Rene also maintains context across conversations, allowing it to remember details and surface things that may need attention later. Additionally, it has a browser, can write code, shop for you, as well as create slides and images. The biggest differentiator with Tomo ’s personal assistant for iMessage is that, instead of being a private assistant that only you interact with, Tomo can become part of group conversations. Also, like other agents, it’s designed to help with goals, accountability, scheduling, and everyday organization. It also has the ability to send reminders, search the web, work with calendars and email, watch videos, and edit photos. Notably, when Fo encounters something it cannot handle on its own, Wajo says it can bring in a human assistant to finish the task. Fo launched publicly in September 2025 with a free tier, while heavier workloads and custom agents are available through a paid Pro offering.

extraction.body: Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person. You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later. While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space. Below are some of the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work. Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check. For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you. Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026. Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan. The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar. Fambot currently connects to Gmail and Google Calendar, with support for Outlook and Apple Calendar planned for the future. The company launched in beta in early September 2026 and has raised $3.5 million in pre-seed funding. The service is currently free during the beta period, but Fambot expects to eventually charge roughly the equivalent of a Netflix subscription. Folk is designed to be an AI assistant you can reach through iMessage, WhatsApp, and Telegram. It can remember personal context, manage reminders, research topics, track flights, handle email, and perform real-world tasks such as restaurant reservations. Instinct first made headlines after raising $350 million at a $2.5 billion valuation. In September 2026, it raised $1 billion , valuing it at $10 billion. The always-available agent can take actions on your behalf, rather than simply answer questions. Users can communicate with Instinct by text or voice and connect it to the apps and services they already use, such as email, calendar, Google Workspace, and more. The company says early users have used Instinct for tasks ranging from planning trips and buying groceries to booking tickets and cancelling subscriptions. In September, Instinct began giving users dedicated email addresses for their assistants. The idea is to let Instinct create and manage accounts on a user’s behalf without filling the user’s personal inbox. The agent can use its address to sign up for services, contact businesses, follow up on requests, and handle tasks that require an email account. (However, this level of autonomy has also raised concerns about privacy and security .) It’s also begun rolling out support for placing calls . Martin is a general-purpose personal assistant reachable through SMS as well as phone, WhatsApp, email, Slack, and its own iOS app. It can help manage calendars, email, reminders, tasks, notes, and communications. It can also act on behalf of users by sending messages or making phone calls, while providing daily summaries of what needs attention. It’s a bit on the pricier side, with subscriptions starting at $21 per month. Ohai is another family assistant focused on helping households manage the constant stream of information and tasks involved in everyday family life. Users can send messages, forward emails, or make voice requests, and the assistant can transform them into schedules, reminders, and plans. It can also coordinate calendars, household chores, and meals across multiple members of a family. It includes a free basic option, but also offers different subscriptions based on family size, starting at $9.99 per month. Similar to the other family-focused agents, the idea behind Ollie is that families already have the information they need, but it lives across school messages, calendars, task lists, and group chats. Ollie aims to bring those pieces together and keep them in sync. It can keep track of calendars, emails, reminders, tasks, and other household details, then deliver relevant information to users through text. Its biggest differentiator from other agents is that Ollie is one of the first mainstream, family-focused AI assistants to achieve SOC 2 compliance, a widely used security standard. Launched in June 2026, Ollie offers a free tier, as well as paid plans starting at $25 per month for 150 messages. A $100-per-month plan includes up to 1,000 messages. Orbits also has an AI assistant that is focused on the household. It works through both the Orbits app and text messaging, and can bring together calendars, lists, and conversations while also carrying out tasks for you. That can include searching the web, making purchases, booking restaurants, changing appointments, and requesting quotes for household services. Additionally, Orbits can remind family members about chores, communicate with service providers, and help coordinate responsibilities beyond the immediate household. There’s a free plan available, which offers features like 15 minutes of calls per month, or there are paid plans, including $25 per month for 30 minutes of calls and $100 per month for 60 minutes. Poke launched in March 2026 as a general-purpose assistant that you can reach through text messaging. It can handle tasks involving calendars, planning, health and fitness, smart-home controls, photos, and other everyday activities. Poke became particularly notable in June 2026 when Apple approved Poke as the first AI agent on the Apple Messages for Business platform. A month later, parent company The Interaction Company of California was acquired by AI coding startup Cognition in a deal valued in the low nine figures. Rene is an AI personal assistant designed to be a user’s “best contact” rather than another productivity agent. It’s text-based and can turn natural-language conversations into tasks, reminders, summaries, and other follow-up actions. Rene also maintains context across conversations, allowing it to remember details and surface things that may need attention later. Additionally, it has a browser, can write code, shop for you, as well as create slides and images. The biggest differentiator with Tomo ’s personal assistant for iMessage is that, instead of being a private assistant that only you interact with, Tomo can become part of group conversations. Also, like other agents, it’s designed to help with goals, accountability, scheduling, and everyday organization. It also has the ability to send reminders, search the web, work with calendars and email, watch videos, and edit photos. Notably, when Fo encounters something it cannot handle on its own, Wajo says it can bring in a human assistant to finish the task. Fo launched publicly in September 2025 with a free tier, while heavier workloads and custom agents are available through a paid Pro offering.

extraction.body: The AI revolution is moving beyond chatbots and into your text messages. A growing ecosystem of AI agents now lives directly in SMS and messaging platforms, offering everything from general assistance to specialized help for families, travel planning, and workplace productivity. This shift represents a major evolution in how we interact with artificial intelligence - making it as simple as sending a text. The latest frontier in AI isn't happening in fancy apps or desktop software - it's taking place in the most basic communication tool we all use: text messages. A new generation of AI agents is embedding directly into SMS and popular messaging platforms, transforming how millions of people access artificial intelligence. Unlike traditional AI assistants that require dedicated apps or specific devices, these text-based agents work with any phone capable of sending messages. Users simply text a number or add a contact, then start conversing with AI systems designed for specific tasks and contexts. Text-based AI agents eliminate these barriers by meeting users where they already spend significant time. Family-focused agents lead this emerging category, helping parents coordinate schedules, track activities, and manage household tasks through group chats. Travel agents powered by AI can handle booking research, itinerary planning, and real-time trip updates via simple text exchanges. Workplace productivity agents integrate with team messaging to automate routine tasks and provide quick information lookups. The technology leverages advances in large language models while working within the constraints of text messaging. These agents must communicate clearly in short bursts, handle context switching between different conversation threads, and maintain personality consistency across extended interactions. Several startups are betting big on this messaging-first approach to AI deployment. It also opens AI access to demographics that might otherwise avoid more complex AI tools. The integration possibilities extend beyond simple SMS to include WhatsApp, Telegram, and other popular messaging services where users already manage personal and professional communications. The shift reflects broader changes in how people expect to interact with technology. Rather than downloading specific apps for every function, users increasingly prefer services that integrate into existing workflows and communication patterns. Security and privacy considerations remain paramount as these services handle sensitive personal and professional information through messaging channels. The messaging-based AI trend also highlights the ongoing evolution of conversational interfaces. While voice assistants like Amazon's Alexa dominated earlier AI adoption waves, text-based interactions offer advantages in privacy, context retention, and multi-tasking scenarios. The emergence of AI agents in text messaging represents a significant shift toward more accessible and integrated artificial intelligence. By removing the friction of separate apps and complex interfaces, these services could accelerate mainstream AI adoption while fundamentally changing how we think about digital assistance. As the technology matures, expect messaging-based AI to become as common as sending a regular text - and potentially much more powerful.

extraction.body: Meta says FDA isn’t sufficient to Muse reading messages. Apple begs to differ. Apple says it is changing its macOS privacy settings to stop third-party app developers from misusing them to access message histories. Friday’s announcement comes two weeks after tech columnist Jason Aten said that Meta’s new general-purpose AI agent Muse sent him an unsolicited notification referencing a thread between him and a co-worker over Apple Messages. Aten said he never granted Muse permissions to read his messages and had assumed they were off-limits. Social media last week blew up with masses of people who agreed and said the incident showed that AI assistants given access to calendars, emails, messages, shopping accounts, and other resources are akin to a skill saw or other power tool. While potentially useful, they can do real damage if not used carefully. Meta CTO David Singleton joined the fray with a rebuttal that appeared solid. For Muse to access Apple Messages, a user must manually give it two privileges. One is full-disk access, a macOS system-level permission. The other is to enable a Messages connector setting in Muse. “The Messages integration in the Muse Mac app is opt in,” Singleton said. “Your Muse can only read Messages content if macOS system-level Full Disk Access is granted and the Messages connector is enabled.” Singleton’s implication was clear. Muse could have read Aten’s Messages communications only if he had enabled both settings, and if so, the columnist had only himself—and certainly not Meta—to blame. Earlier this week, I spoke to macOS security expert Patrick Wardle, who questioned Singleton’s denial. His reasoning: “From a technical point of view, with FDA (full-disk access), any (non-root file), is readable, browsing history, browser cookies, chats, etc etc etc.” I asked Meta how Muse couldn’t read messages when the app had full disk access, while every other app with that privilege could. Meta PR’s only response was to requote Singleton saying: “The Messages integration in the Muse Mac App is opt-in. Your Muse can only read Messages content if macOS system-level Full Disk Access is granted and the Messages connector is enabled.” Now, Apple is setting the record straight. In explaining why it was going to make changes to the FDA permission setting, the company wrote: Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems—including files, mail, messages, and even browsing history—without users’ full knowledge and understanding. For communication apps, this can also compromise the privacy of the people users are communicating with. As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially. We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy. Apple didn’t name Meta, Muse, or any other app or developer by name. Even though there are no known reports of other apps abusing FDA to read messages and browsing history, it’s certainly possible Friday’s statement wasn’t referring to the Muse incident. Then again, the timing of the announcement—coming on the heels of a major social media uproar—makes the possibility likely. And at a minimum, Apple’s statements seem to contradict Singleton’s denial that it’s not possible for Muse to read Messages content without the connector enabled. Meta PR didn’t respond to questions sent Friday. Apple’s announcement came 11 days after Wardle disclosed a Muse configuration that allowed any app or code running on a Mac—including commands injected through the increasingly effective ClickFix attacks—to take full control of the AI assistant . From there, the attacker could access the same resources Muse could. It also comes after Amazon blocked Muse from its platform because, Amazon said, all such apps “should operate openly and respect service provider decisions about whether or not to participate.” Taken together, the events suggest that Muse may not be worthy of the extraordinary access it must have to work as billed by Meta. People who use the assistant should configure permissions carefully, though as Aten’s experience suggests, that precaution only goes so far. Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

coreStoryFacts.text: For Muse to access Apple Messages, a user must manually give it two privileges.
One is full-disk access, a macOS system-level permission.

Apple’s announcement came 11 days after Wardle disclosed a Muse configuration that allowed any app or code running on a Mac—including commands injected through the increasingly effective ClickFix attacks—to take full control of the AI assistant .
From there, the attacker could access the same resources Muse could.
It also comes after Amazon blocked Muse from its platform because, Amazon said, all such apps “should operate openly and respect service provider decisions about whether or not to participate.”

Friday’s announcement comes two weeks after tech columnist Jason Aten said that Meta’s new general-purpose AI agent Muse sent him an unsolicited notification referencing a thread between him and a co-worker over Apple Messages.
In explaining why it was going to make changes to the FDA permission setting, the company wrote:
Apple says it is changing its macOS privacy settings to stop third-party app developers from misusing them to access message histories.
As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially.
Meta says FDA isn’t sufficient to Muse reading messages.
Apple didn’t name Meta, Muse, or any other app or developer by name.
Even though there are no known reports of other apps abusing FDA to read messages and browsing history, it’s certainly possible Friday’s statement wasn’t referring to the Muse incident.
Then again, the timing of the announcement—coming on the heels of a major social media uproar—makes the possibility likely.
Meta PR didn’t respond to questions sent Friday.

extraction.body: Meta says FDA isn’t sufficient to Muse reading messages. Apple begs to differ. Apple says it is changing its macOS privacy settings to stop third-party app developers from misusing them to access message histories. Friday’s announcement comes two weeks after tech columnist Jason Aten said that Meta’s new general-purpose AI agent Muse sent him an unsolicited notification referencing a thread between him and a co-worker over Apple Messages. Aten said he never granted Muse permissions to read his messages and had assumed they were off-limits. Social media last week blew up with masses of people who agreed and said the incident showed that AI assistants given access to calendars, emails, messages, shopping accounts, and other resources are akin to a skill saw or other power tool. While potentially useful, they can do real damage if not used carefully. Meta CTO David Singleton joined the fray with a rebuttal that appeared solid. For Muse to access Apple Messages, a user must manually give it two privileges. One is full-disk access, a macOS system-level permission. The other is to enable a Messages connector setting in Muse. “The Messages integration in the Muse Mac app is opt in,” Singleton said. “Your Muse can only read Messages content if macOS system-level Full Disk Access is granted and the Messages connector is enabled.” Singleton’s implication was clear. Muse could have read Aten’s Messages communications only if he had enabled both settings, and if so, the columnist had only himself—and certainly not Meta—to blame. Earlier this week, I spoke to macOS security expert Patrick Wardle, who questioned Singleton’s denial. His reasoning: “From a technical point of view, with FDA (full-disk access), any (non-root file), is readable, browsing history, browser cookies, chats, etc etc etc.” I asked Meta how Muse couldn’t read messages when the app had full disk access, while every other app with that privilege could. Meta PR’s only response was to requote Singleton saying: “The Messages integration in the Muse Mac App is opt-in. Your Muse can only read Messages content if macOS system-level Full Disk Access is granted and the Messages connector is enabled.” Now, Apple is setting the record straight. In explaining why it was going to make changes to the FDA permission setting, the company wrote: Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems—including files, mail, messages, and even browsing history—without users’ full knowledge and understanding. For communication apps, this can also compromise the privacy of the people users are communicating with. As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially. We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy. Apple didn’t name Meta, Muse, or any other app or developer by name. Even though there are no known reports of other apps abusing FDA to read messages and browsing history, it’s certainly possible Friday’s statement wasn’t referring to the Muse incident. Then again, the timing of the announcement—coming on the heels of a major social media uproar—makes the possibility likely. And at a minimum, Apple’s statements seem to contradict Singleton’s denial that it’s not possible for Muse to read Messages content without the connector enabled. Meta PR didn’t respond to questions sent Friday. Apple’s announcement came 11 days after Wardle disclosed a Muse configuration that allowed any app or code running on a Mac—including commands injected through the increasingly effective ClickFix attacks—to take full control of the AI assistant . From there, the attacker could access the same resources Muse could. It also comes after Amazon blocked Muse from its platform because, Amazon said, all such apps “should operate openly and respect service provider decisions about whether or not to participate.” Taken together, the events suggest that Muse may not be worthy of the extraordinary access it must have to work as billed by Meta. People who use the assistant should configure permissions carefully, though as Aten’s experience suggests, that precaution only goes so far. sources.title: Apple to flag AI requests for Mac data after Meta’s Muse complaints - Crypto Briefing
passages: Apple is tightening one of the most powerful permissions on the Mac.
The company says AI requests for Mac data will become more visible to users, with new controls and explicit prompts around a setting called Full Disk Access. \n The timing is not subtle.

The move follows complaints that Meta ’s Muse AI agent allegedly read private Messages content without the proper permissions. 
 

 What Apple is changing 
 Apple announced the macOS updates on October 2, 2026.
As autonomous AI tools grow more capable, Apple argued, the dangers tied to broad data access evolve right alongside them. \n Advertisement \n SEARCH Searching...
Complaints about its data access surfaced shortly afterward.
For Meta specifically, the Muse launch on Mac got off to a bumpy start.
For Apple, the update reinforces a brand built heavily on privacy.
It also quietly positions Apple as the gatekeeper for AI agents on its platform.
Any company that wants its agent to operate deeply on a Mac will now have to persuade users through a more deliberate permission process.
Apple said granting this permission will now require “very explicit user action.” The stated goal is to stop developers from misusing that level of access.
The company framed the update as a response to shifting risks.
The episode highlights a long-standing split in Apple’s ecosystem.
On iOS and iPadOS, apps live under stricter sandboxing rules that keep them walled off from each other’s data.
The most prominent came from technology columnist Jason Aten.

extraction.body: The ICBA, which represents small and community banks in the U.S., sued banking regulator OCC, arguing it exceeded its authority by granting national trust bank charters to crypto companies.
